The session begins.

The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."

James turns his shoulder to the barrel. The slap of the cards keeps going behind him, steady as a pulse: *find the lady, friends, a silver says you've still got your eye*. The cat hears what he says under his breath. It comes back against his boot and stays there, pressed to the leather, its tail low now and twitching at the tip.

He gives the shuttered stalls one glance. Between them, past the last good lamp, someone leans against a post with his hood up and his arms folded. He isn't moving. His head is turned toward the barrel, not the queue.

Then James is at the trestle.

Up close Sergeant Marrow looks older than her voice. There are grey threads at her temples, and a smear of ink runs from her thumb to her wrist where she has wiped her eyes too often. She looks at his nod and holds the look a moment longer than she has to. Then she looks down at the pay slip. She tilts it toward the lamp to see the seal and leaves the figure alone.

"Tethyr," she says. "Zaranda's." It's neither a question nor a compliment. She pushes the slip back to him with two fingers.

A thick ledger lies open beside the chalkboard, held flat with a stone against the river wind. She dips her pen and writes him in: *Worgen, J. — Tethyr via Beregost — work.* Her hand is small and quick. The names above his run back up the page in the same ink. A few of them have a small chalk cross in the margin, rubbed in by a fingertip and not by the chalk. She turns the page before the ink is dry, and the crosses go with it.

"Fist takes anyone with two hands and a pulse," she says. "Recruiting's at the Seatower, mornings. Pay's late. Has been for a year." She sets the pen down. "You want honest caravan work, go through Basilisk Gate and ask at the wagon yards on the left. The masters post their boards there. Ignore anyone who comes up to you first."

She glances past his shoulder at the barrel, the waistcoat and the drovers leaning in, then back at him.

"You turned your back on him," she says. "Most don't." She waits a moment as if she might say more, then picks up the chalk. "Beds are cheaper this side of the wall. Cleaner the other side. Foot traffic's free. Next."

The man behind James shifts his bundle. At James's boot, the cat hasn't moved its ears from the stalls.

Sergeant Marrow's chalk stops above the board for a moment.

"Then you're ahead of most of them," she says. She doesn't look up, and she doesn't smile back. "Next."

The queue closes behind him like water. The bridge takes him in: wheel ruts worn into the stones, a fishwife packing up her board, cooking smoke from a window just over his head. The shops lean in so close on both sides that the river is only a sound under the planking and a smell of tar. Up ahead the span climbs toward the dark bulk of Wyrm's Rock in the middle of the river, and somewhere past it Basilisk Gate. The lamps get further apart the farther he goes.

The two shuttered stalls are on his left, on his way. They're coming up.

A dozen paces in, he bends and lifts the cat. It goes limp in his hands the way cats do when they've decided to allow something, then settles on his shoulder facing backwards, claws hooked lightly into the cloak. Its whiskers brush his ear.

Its answer doesn't come as words. It comes as pictures and smells, sorted into something like speech.

*Him: onion. Old ale. Oil, like the rag for your blade.* A pause, and the scent of a man who hasn't changed his shirt. *Still. Very still. Cat at a mousehole, not hungry. Bored-waiting.*

Then a picture, seen low from a cat's height a minute ago: the hooded head barely moving, and his lips working each time the man in the waistcoat took a coin off the barrel.

*One. At the post, one. Many feet everywhere, can't tell more.*

The cat goes quiet. Then James feels its whole body tighten on his shoulder.

Behind him, back at the barrel, a drover gives a whoop. "There she is! Eye like a hawk, friend, eye like a hawk!" Coins clink into a hand as the man in the waistcoat counts out the winnings, light and quick.

*Wrong,* the cat sends, and the fur along its spine rises under his collar. *Not him. The coins. The ones from the barrel-man's hand. Wet cellar. Old candles.* Its ears stay pinned toward the sound. *Fur doesn't like.*

The drover is still laughing back there. Up ahead, ten paces off now, the hooded man shifts his weight against the post. He's still watching the barrel past James's shoulder, as if James were just another body walking by.

*Remember,* the cat sends back. It comes as the smell itself, held up like a mouse brought to the doorstep: wet stone, wax gone old in the dark. Then, firmly: *Tell. Even sleeping. Paw on face.*

James comes level with the post and shifts his pack strap, the way any tired man does fifty feet into a long bridge. One sideways look.

The hood is brown wool, darker at the edge where a hand keeps pulling it forward. Under it he sees a stubbled jaw and a nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry. The man is younger than his stillness made him seem, maybe twenty-five. His folded arms aren't really folded. His left hand is tucked into his right elbow, and in his right fingers he holds a length of dirty string with knots spaced along it. A knife hangs on his belt in a sheath worn pale at the mouth. Beside it is a flat leather purse, empty enough to lie flat. He has no badge, no colours, nothing a Fist sergeant would write down.

James's eyes go back to the road. He keeps the same pace.

Once the post is behind him he tips his head. The cat's weight shifts on his shoulder, and its view comes to him faintly, like a picture held at arm's length: lamplight, the hooded man getting smaller, the barrel beyond him, the drover still pocketing his coppers.

*He looks. You,* the cat sends. *Then me. Then barrel again.* There's a pause, and the picture tightens. Back at the barrel the card man has taken another silver off someone. The string moves between the hooded man's fingers, and he ties another knot. *Ties. Every coin, ties. Doesn't follow. Bored.*

The bridge carries James on. A chandler is putting his shutters up. A woman shakes a rug out of a window overhead and doesn't look to see who is under it. Wyrm's Rock rises dark out of the middle of the span, with a few lit windows in its walls. The road splits around its base, and beyond it the lamps of Basilisk Gate are a line of orange in the dusk.

At the foot of the Rock a boy with a satchel of broadsheets stands on an upturned crate and shouts in a voice that's already gone hoarse:

"*Baldur's Mouth!* Council squabbles over the Trade Way tolls! Rope-walk fire in the Lower City, three hurt! Another one pulled out under the Crossing this morning, coin in his teeth, Umberlee's taking her due! Two coppers, the Mouth, two coppers!"

A porter buys one, glances at it and tucks it under his arm. Beside the crate, a girl with a bucket of river-washed cups stops with her back to the stones. She isn't looking at the boy. She's looking at the cat on James's shoulder.

The boy takes the two coppers without stopping his shout. He bites one out of habit, drops both into his satchel and hands down a folded sheet that's still damp from the press. "Ain't any change, mister, it's two. Ta." Then he turns back to the bridge: "*Baldur's Mouth!* Coin in his teeth!"

James tucks the paper under his arm.

The girl hasn't moved. She's maybe sixteen, thin in the way of someone who eats last. Her sleeves are wet to the elbow and there's a rag tied over her hair. She holds the bucket of cups in front of her with both hands. When the cat turns its head on James's shoulder and looks straight back at her, she doesn't flinch, and her eyes stay on it a moment longer than his joke would earn.

"Wasn't going to buy him," she says.

*Smell her,* he sends.

The answer comes in layers, the way the cat sorts a room. *River. Lye-soap, hands. Fish, old, from the cups. Bread, a little, eaten fast.* A pause, and then its nose works harder against his ear. *Pocket. Her apron, left side. Small. Wet cellar. Candles.* Its claws tighten in the cloak. *Same as barrel-coins. One. Maybe two. Not hers-smell. Someone else's hands on it first.*

The girl shifts the bucket from one hip to the other.

"Rooms," she says. She talks fast, like she's been holding it in. "Don't take Tessaly's, over the chandler. Floor's gone soft and she charges for the bugs. Halfway House by the Rock's all right if you've got the silver, and they don't let anyone up the stairs who isn't paid. Inside the wall's cleaner. Mermaid's by the docks, but you'd want a knife for that." She glances back down the bridge toward the checkpoint lamps, where Dov's barrel is out of sight now. "And you know about the barrels already. I saw you. You walked right past."

Two porters push between them with a hand-cart. She waits for them to go by and steps half a pace closer. Her voice drops.

"My brother doesn't walk past. Pim. He's twelve. He plays the barrels, all of them, the one by the checkpoint and the two up by the fish steps. And he *wins*, mister. Every night he wins. Coppers. And then his shoe splits, and the stove spits on his arm, and yesterday a cart near took his foot off." She stops and swallows. "The man they pulled out this morning won too. Three nights running at the fish steps. Everyone saw him. He was buying drinks with it."

Her eyes go to the cat again, then to James's hands, then finally to his face.

"Cats don't ride people like that. Not facing backwards, watching. That's a familiar." It isn't a question until the end. "You're something. A wizard, or a priest, or — something that knows about luck. Aren't you?"

She follows him out of the stream of people to the Rock's wall. The foot traffic goes past an arm's length away. She keeps the bucket between them.

When he says *nobody wins every night for free*, her face loosens a little, as if she'd been braced for him to laugh.

"That's what I told Pim," she says. "He said I was jealous."

Then he nods at her apron and she goes still. Her eyes don't go to him. They go to the cat. "It told you." It isn't a question. She sets the bucket down against the wall, keeps it between her feet, and digs in her left pocket. She brings out two coppers and holds them on her flat palm under the lamp, the way you'd hold something out to a dog you don't trust.

They're ordinary Gate coppers, thin from handling, the ship on one face worn almost smooth. At a glance there's nothing wrong with them. Then she tips her hand and the lamplight runs along the rims. Each one has a tiny mark set into the edge, smaller than a grain of barley. It's black, as if it had been burned in rather than cut: a stem and two branching tines. An antler.

James knows that shape. Anyone who has spent years at southern card tables has heard men curse it under their breath when the dice go against them. The Maid of Misfortune wears antlers, black on red. Beshaba. The Lady's sister, and nobody at a table ever says her name loud.

On his shoulder the cat leans out until its whiskers nearly touch her fingers. *Cellar. Candles. Same as barrel.* A pause while its nose works. *Warm. Like a thing held in a hand. No hand.* Its tail lashes once against his back.

"They're warm," Wren says, as if she'd heard it. "Always. I've been in the river to my knees all afternoon with them in my pocket, and they're warm." She closes her fingers over them. "I won't spend them. I can't make my hand do it. I threw one off the bridge on Tuesday." She swallows. "He came home with three that night."

She puts them back in the pocket and wipes her palm on her apron, hard.

"Pim's at the fish steps. Now. He takes the cups back up for me at the end of the day, and then he plays. I told him not to and he went anyway." She jerks her chin north along the span, past the Rock. "Round the river side of the Rock, down where the boats tie up. You'll smell it before you see it."

"The man this morning was Corran. From Elturel. He came down on the barges last spring and carried baskets for the fishwives. He played both barrels at the steps, whichever had the shorter line. It didn't matter which one. He won at both." She stops to think, and her mouth goes flat. "Dov's too, the first night, by the checkpoint. I saw him. The barrels changed and he kept winning."

"They laid him out on the steps this morning. He had a copper in his teeth. I saw it before the Fist took it, but I couldn't see the edge."

A cart rumbles past and she waits for the noise to die.

"I'm Wren." She picks the bucket back up, both hands, in front of her. "If you know something about luck, will you come and look at him? Before he plays?"

Wren doesn't say anything to *yes*. She looks at him once, quickly, the way someone checks a rope they've just been thrown, then turns and goes. She walks fast and the cups clink in the bucket.

She takes his three things one at a time over her shoulder.

"Soldier from Tethyr. Fine." A few steps on: "I haven't been crying." She says it flat, and she doesn't wipe her face to prove it. At the third she slows half a step and her eyes go to his hand at his collar, to the cord there. "He'll ask you to stake him. He asks everyone with boots on. Tell him no and he'll call you a coward. He's twelve."

The road splits around the base of the Rock. She takes the river side, where the lamps give out and the wall drops away into a stair cut into the stone. Wind comes straight off the Chionthar here, cold and wet. James tastes it before he sees anything: fish gone soft in the heat of the day, tar, river mud, smoke from a brazier, and under that the sweet rot of guts somebody hasn't sluiced off yet.

The cat goes off his shoulder in one soft drop and is gone along the foot of the wall, low, a darker shape against dark stone.

The fish steps are a broad stone stair going down to the water, slick and scaled with silver. Skiffs knock against the bottom landing. Lanterns hang on poles, and the fishwives on the middle steps are packing up, scraping boards, tipping buckets of heads over the side for the gulls. Halfway down, one wide step is empty. Everyone walks around it. A fish basket has been set there upside down, with a twist of dry straw tucked under its rim.

"That's where they put him," Wren says without stopping. "Corran."

There are two barrels at the top of the stair, one on each side, like gateposts.

On the left a big man with a split lip runs three walnut shells and a dried pea across the barrel head. He keeps up a low patter and his fingers move fast. On the right a halfling woman in a man's coat rattles a pair of bone dice in a leather cup and calls *high or low, high or low* in a voice like a creaking hinge. Each barrel has a few people around it: porters done for the day, a boatman, two boys who should be home.

The cat's report comes in pieces while James is still on the stairs.

*Knot-man: no. Nobody tying. Nobody still. Everyone moving, everyone looking at hands.*

*Shells-man. Pouch on belt, back side. Cellar. Candles.* A pause. *Dice-woman, too. Pouch in coat. Same. Same-same. Both.*

Then the picture sharpens, seen low from under a coil of rope by the left-hand barrel. It's a boy's legs. One shoe is split along the side and tied shut with string, and above it is a bare shin with a bruise going yellow. A cuff hangs over a rag bound around a forearm. *Smells like her,* the cat sends. *Lye. River. Cups. Small. Her-but-small.* Its nose works. *Hand closed. In hand: cellar. Candles. Many. Warm.*

The boy is third in the line at the shells.

Wren has seen him too. She stops at the top step so suddenly the cups slosh. Her free hand comes back and catches a fold of James's sleeve without her seeming to decide to. She doesn't call out to him.

The man at the front of the line puts down a copper and loses it. The big man scoops it into his apron with a grunt of sympathy, and the shells start moving again.

Pim is two from the front.

James goes down the steps ahead of her. His boots make no sound on the wet stone, and the fishwives don't look up. Pim is one from the front now. The man ahead of him is laying a copper on the barrel head, and the big man's hands have already started on the shells, *round she goes, where she stops* — when a hand settles on the boy's shoulder from the river side.

Pim jumps. He turns his head and looks up at a stranger in an old soldier's cloak who has stepped between him and the barrel without being asked. The boy has his sister's narrow face, with none of her caution in it yet.

James looks past him, once, straight at the shells-man. The big man's fingers keep moving, but his patter goes flat for a word or two. His eyes come up, hold James's for a moment and go back down to the shells.

The silver comes out of James's pouch and catches the lantern light.

Pim looks at the coin and then at the hand holding it. His sister is in his face, wary and quick, and he's doing sums with it.

"Silver," he says. "A whole one. For a *room*." He works it through, and you can see him find no catch he can name. "Halfway House, then. By the Rock. They don't rob you, they just charge." He glances at the shells once more. The man in front has lost, and the big man is scooping the copper into his apron. Pim's closed fist goes into his pocket, and it stays closed. "And the yards in the morning's easy, it's just through the gate and left. I'd have told you that for nothing." He catches himself. "But I won't."

He steps out of the line. The boatman behind him moves up into his place without a word.

"Your loss, little man," the shells-man says, mild and low. He doesn't look at James again, and the shells start moving under his fingers. *Round she goes.*

Wren comes down the last two steps with the bucket held in front of her. Pim sees her, and his shoulders go up around his ears.

"He's paying me," he tells her, before she can open her mouth. "Silver. It's a job." She doesn't answer. She looks at James instead, one quick look, and shifts the bucket to her other hip.

From somewhere behind the rope coil, the cat: *Warm ones. In his pocket now. Still with him.* A beat. *Barrel-man's hand stopped. When you looked.*

Pim has already started up the steps toward the Rock, walking backwards so he can talk. He's a boy who has just been hired and wants to sound like it.

"You were a soldier, yeah? You've got the cloak." His eyes go to James's belt, to his hands, to the pouch the silver came out of. "Soldiers all play. Corran said so. He said in the barges they played every night." He grins, and it's crooked, because his lip is chapped. "You'll stake me tomorrow, then? One game. I'd win it for you. I *always* win."

Pim stops on the step above him when the silver comes out again. James holds it out in the open, under the lantern on the pole, where the two fishwives scraping their boards can see. One of them looks up, sees a coin go from a grown man's hand to Wren's brother's, and looks back at her board with her mouth pursed, as if she's filing it away.

Pim takes it fast. He turns it over once and doesn't bite it. He keeps his eyes on James's face while his thumb finds the milled edge. Then it goes into his other pocket, the right one. The left one stays shut.

The *no* lands on him and he takes it like a slap he expected. His grin goes crooked and stays.

"A lady," he says. "Must be some lady." He looks past James to his sister, ready for her to side with him or against him so he can be angry either way.

Wren doesn't give him either. She shifts the bucket to her other hip. "He walked past Dov's," she says. "Didn't even look. I saw." That's all she says, and Pim has nothing to push against, so he turns and climbs.

James keeps his voice low on the next few steps. He names the split shoe, the stove, the cart, and nods at the rag on the boy's arm. Pim keeps climbing and doesn't turn round. His shoulders tell it anyway. They come up when James says *the bill*, and they're still up when James says *called in*.

"Everyone's shoes split," Pim says to the step in front of him. "It's a bridge."

Two steps from the top, the string holding his shoe together lets go.

He doesn't even notice it break. His heel slides out on the fish-slick stone, his weight goes back, and his arms fly out. Wren drops the bucket handle and grabs a fistful of his collar. The cups crash against each other and one jumps out and breaks on the step. Pim gets his feet under him again, red to the ears.

From inside his left pocket, as he jerks upright, comes a small dull chink of coppers knocking together.

*Warm,* the cat sends. It's come up the stair behind them, low against the wall, eyes on the boy's pocket. *Warmer. When he fell. Like breath.*

Wren lets go of his collar and picks the broken pieces off the step one at a time. She puts them in the bucket, not over the side. She doesn't look at James.

Pim crouches, knots the string again with quick angry fingers, and stands. "Slippery," he says. Then, after a few more steps and a lot more quietly, to nobody: "Corran never won nothing on the barges. Not once, all the way down from Elturel. He said so." He hears himself and shuts his mouth.

---

The Halfway House is built into the Rock's flank on the city side, four narrow storeys of timber and old stone. It leans against the fortress the way a tired man leans on a wall. There's a lamp over the door. Just inside the door a stair goes straight up, and a woman sits on the third step as if the step were hers. She has forearms like a baker's, a slate in her lap and a short ash cudgel lying across her knees like knitting.

Wren closes her hand over the two coppers the moment they touch her palm, cold and plain. She weighs them for a moment the way Marga weighed the silver. Then they go into the right side of her apron, the side that has nothing in it.

"Sale," she says. At *harder dealer than your brother* one corner of her mouth moves and then stops, as if it hadn't asked her first.

On the table her two marked coins don't move. The threads do. James feels two more hairs come round and settle on him among the others, the way the thirteen did. Sixteen run off south into the dark now, gathered in the same far fist. This time nothing at the other end pulls. It stays slack and still.

Then he says it out loud: *the fourteenth is Pim's. I hold it; I don't own it. Witnessed.* Pim doesn't look at his sister. He watches her mouth, waiting for her to agree.

"Witnessed," Wren says. "It's his."

Pim lets out a breath through his nose. When James tells him he was right about the bag, the boy's chin comes up and stays up. He tries not to grin and only half manages.

"Told you. Brown sack, drawstring, the short one tied it." He shrugs, the way grown men shrug when they're right. "Sergeant'll have it. Fist keeps everything. My da said they've got a room full of dead men's boots in the Seatower."

James unknots the silk scrap from his component pouch and spreads it on the bare wood. With the edge of his hand he sweeps the coppers onto it. They scrape and click together, and then they're in a heap. They don't lie still. Each one turns a little in the pile until it finds its line, and the heap ends up leaning toward the back wall. He ties the corners tight. He tears a strip off one corner of the silk, twists Corran's coin into it on its own and knots it shut. In the twist the coin keeps pushing, slow and patient, looking for a lap that's back across the table.

He works the bundle into the outer pocket of his pack and buckles the flap. The buckle's tongue comes off in his fingers. It doesn't bend first. It's an old brass prong that has held for years, and now it's a bit of metal in his palm. The flap hangs open on the coins.

Nobody says anything about it.

On the threshold the cat has backed up a full body-length. It's sitting with its tail wrapped round its feet as tight as a knot. *All in the bag now,* it sends. *All breathing. At you.* A pause, and then a picture held up for him: the pack in front of him, seen from the floor, with a darker warmth inside it like a coal in ash. *Don't sleep on that side.*

James tells them about the tug on the line, and that he'd rather the net moved to him. Wren's eyes go to the open flap of the pack and then to his face. She doesn't argue with him. She looks like someone who has finally seen a bill paid by somebody else, and doesn't like how it feels.

When he asks where they sleep, Pim answers first, quick and proud.

"Hesk's. The cooperage, river side of the Rock, past the fish steps. Loft over the barrel shed." He jerks his thumb at the wall, roughly south and down. "It's got a *hatch*."

"It's got a ladder," Wren says. Her voice is flat. "And a hatch with a bar you drop across from the inside. No lock. Hesk lets us have it for me sweeping the shavings out." She shifts on the bench. Her foot finds the bucket on the floor. "The bar's good. It's oak. Nobody's ever come up." Then, lower, because she has started telling the truth tonight and can't seem to stop: "But the ladder's half off its pegs since Thursday. Pim's foot went through the third rung."

Pim scratches the rag on his arm and looks at the fire.

The pot has gone quiet on its hook. Downstairs, on the third step, Marga coughs once. The house settles around them, dry wood and onions, and the black stone of the Rock is cool at their backs.

James leaves the brass tongue by his bowl. Pim looks at it, then at the pack, and goes back to his barley a little faster. Wren doesn't touch her spoon at all until James is at the door.

The stair is darker going down than it was coming up. The rushlight on the landing has burned low. The cat comes after him, keeping two steps behind, and it keeps the stair rail between itself and the pack hanging from his left hand.

Marga hasn't moved. The slate is in her lap, the cudgel across her knees, and the street door below her is shut and barred now. She hears him stop two steps above her and doesn't turn round until he's done talking. Then she twists on the step, looks up at his face, at the pack held out away from his body, and at the flap hanging open.

"Your flap's open," she says.

She waits to see if he'll explain it. When he doesn't, she lets it go.

"There's the box room. Top of the house, under the slates, past your own door. One cot. They'll sleep head to foot, they've done worse. It has a lock, a key, and a window that doesn't open, so nobody comes in that way and nobody falls out of it." She taps the slate. "Five silver. Same as yours. A room's a room."

"Not the kitchen floor. Dalla comes in at fourth bell to light the ovens, and she steps on whatever's down there. I don't sell floors." She pauses. "Not even at room price."

She turns back to face the door. It's as if the part about the boy's pocket needed less of her attention than the price did.

"I don't ask what's in pockets, soldier. I ask what's on the step." Her thumb rubs a smudge off the slate. "That boy's been on my step before with coppers. Never with silver. He'll tell me himself before breakfast, whether I ask or not. You'd have to sew his mouth shut."

Upstairs a spoon scrapes the bottom of a bowl. Marga holds out her hand flat over the step below her, palm up and empty, and waits.

Marga's hand closes over the five silver and they go under the apron with the rest. She chalks a second mark on the slate, a little apart from the first.

"Twelve," she says. It's an entry, not a remark.

She listens to the part about the buckle with her eyes on the open flap. "Harl the strapmaker, two doors past the chandler. He opens when he's sober, so early." That's all she offers on the subject.

From somewhere inside the apron she brings out an iron key on a loop of greasy string and lays it in his palm. It's heavy for its size.

When he gets to the brown hood and the broken nose, she twists round on the step again and looks up at him for longer than she did over the price.

"Brown hood and a broken nose is half the Crossing." She turns back to the door. "Anybody asks at my door, they get what everybody gets. Paid, gone up, and what's upstairs is upstairs. I don't need asking to say it." She settles the cudgel across her knees. "Or paying."

---

When he gets back to the kitchen the bowls are empty. Pim has wiped his round with a crust and is now eyeing the bottom of the pot. Wren is already standing, with the bucket in front of her.

"Box room," James tells them, and holds up the key.

Pim looks at the key, then at James, then at the ceiling as if he can see through it to the slates. "A *room*. With a key." He's on his feet. "That's five silver, that is. Marga's rooms are five." He does the sum on his fingers and frowns at it, because there's nothing in it for him and he can't find the catch. He shuts his mouth on whatever he was going to ask.

Wren looks at the key for a long moment, then at the pack hanging off his left side. She doesn't say anything. She goes past him onto the stair with the bucket held high.

They climb past the second landing and past a door with a number burned into it, his own. The stair gets narrower and steeper until it's almost a ladder with handrails. The cat goes ahead of them. It stops at every landing and sniffs at the shadows, and sends him nothing but *dust, dry, old mouse, gone* the whole way up.

The box room door is low and thick, set right under the pitch of the roof. Inside there's barely space for the cot along one wall and a stool along the other. A small square of thick, greenish glass is mortared into the gable, and the lamps of the Crossing show through it as a smear far below. The air is warm from the day's sun on the slates and smells of straw ticking.

Pim stoops in under the beam and sits down on the cot. He bounces once. "It's short," he reports. "My feet'll be in her face."

"They always are," Wren says.

James puts the key in her hand. She closes her fingers on it and looks at him over the bucket, and for a moment she seems about to say a thank-you she can't afford. What she says is, "Night, mister." Then she pulls the door to.

The bolt goes across inside the lock with a solid iron *clack*. A moment later he hears her try the handle from the inside, rattling it twice to be sure. He can hear Pim through the planks: "*Five silver*, Wren—" Then Wren hushes him.

The cat sits down on the top step beside James's boot, a careful body-length from the pack. Its tail is wrapped round its feet.

Below them the house creaks and settles. Marga's on her step, the street door is barred, and his own room is one flight down. It's nearly nine, and the rest of the night is his to spend however he likes.

The door of his room has a number burned into it and a lock that turns stiff on the second try. Then it holds. The room is a step bigger than the box room above. There's a bed with a straw tick, a chair, a peg by the door and one small window over the river, its glass gone wavy with age. The Crossing's lamps lie below it like coals.

The pack goes in the far corner under the window, flap to the wall. Rapier and crossbow go on the peg, the cloak over the chair. He pulls off his boots and sits on the side of the bed farthest from the corner.

The cat looks at the pat on the blanket and then at the door, as if Marga might be behind it. Then it jumps up. It doesn't curl up by his hip. It lies down along the edge of the tick between him and the corner, chin on its paws, eyes on the pack. *Paw on face,* it sends. It sounds like a promise.

James takes the Lady's coin out of his collar. The bead of water on her cheek is still there, cold as a nail. He holds the coin in both hands the way he held it that last night and makes his report.

For a while the room gives nothing back. Wood ticks as the roof cools. Somewhere below, a door shuts.

Then the pressure under his breastbone comes back, the same weight as in the kitchen, someone leaning over his shoulder. This time she doesn't just look. It feels like a hand laid flat over both of his on the coin, warm, the way a friend at the table covers your hand when you're about to say too much. It isn't a word, but it's an answer: *yes. This.* Something in it is close to amusement.

Then her attention moves off him. He feels it the way you feel a gambler beside you stop watching your cards and look across the table. It runs past the corner and the pack, through the wall, and south along the sixteen hairs into the dark. It settles on whatever holds the other end. It's the look of someone sizing up a stake, not someone pitying the one who lost it. It holds there a long moment.

Then she's gone, and the weight under his breastbone is gone with her.

The bead of water on the coin has dried. The Lady's cheek is just worn silver.

On the tick the cat's tail flicks once. *Someone was here. Warm. Like yours at the table.* A pause. *Looked at the bag. Not afraid of it.* Another pause, less sure. *Wanted it.*

A draught comes through the old window frame and tips the folded *Mouth* off the chair onto the floor. It lands half open, ink side up, on a column of small type under the heading SAILINGS & ARRIVALS. He hasn't read it.

The house is quiet and the door is locked. The rest of the night is his, whether he reads, sleeps, or something else.

messages.text:
I keep my eyes off the barrel and the three cards — I make a point of it, actually, turning so the waistcoat is behind my shoulder. The slap of the cards is a sound I know too well; it goes right down the spine.

To the cat, under my breath: "Not now. Stay close." I give the two shuttered stalls one glance, no more — I'll ask it what it smelled once we're through.

Then I step up to the trestle table and give the sergeant an easy, tired soldier's nod — one person who's been on duty too long to another.

"James Worgen. Out of Tethyr, by way of Beregost. Served in Queen Zaranda's infantry, then scouts; since then, caravan work and the like." I set the regimental pay slip on the table where she can see the seal, not the number. "No employer waiting on me. I'm here to find work — guards, escort, that sort of thing — and a bed tonight. Where does a man with a clean record and his own kit go to get hired honestly in this city, Sergeant? The Fist, or someone else?"

I take the slip back and tuck it inside my coat, and give her the smallest shrug. "I've already lost everything I was going to lose at that game, Sergeant. There's nothing left on me for him." A half-smile, no more. "Thank you for the yards. And for the warning."

I step out of her lamplight and let the queue close behind me, walking the way she pointed — toward Basilisk Gate — without hurrying and without looking back at the barrel. Once I'm a dozen paces along, I reach down and scoop the cat up onto my shoulder, the way a man does with a cat he's tired of tripping over, and ask it silently, mind to mind: *The one by the post, hood up, watching the card man. What's he to you — did you smell something, or is it just the way he's standing? Is he alone?*

I keep walking. Whatever the barrel-man is paying out, it isn't my money, and it isn't my errand — not yet.

*Remember that smell,* I tell the cat. *Wet cellar, old candles. If you ever catch it again — on a coin, on a man, on a door — you tell me. Even if I'm asleep.*

As I come level with the post I do what any tired traveller does: I adjust the strap of my pack and glance sideways at the man leaning there, the way you glance at anyone standing still in a street where everyone else is moving. One look to fix his face — hood, jaw, hands, what's on his belt — and then my eyes go back to the road ahead. I don't slow and I don't speed up.

Only once he's behind me, I tilt my head toward the cat on my shoulder, so it can watch him over my back while I keep walking toward Wyrm's Rock and the gate beyond it.

I fish two coppers out of my belt pouch and hold them out to the boy without breaking stride much — a man who's learned you buy the local sheet first and ask questions second. "The Mouth. Keep the change if there is any." I tuck it under my arm; I'll read it by lamplight once I've got a bed.

The girl with the cups I don't pretend not to see. I let her look, and the cat looks back at her from my shoulder. "He's not for sale," I say, mild, with half a smile. "Though he'd tell you otherwise if he could talk." I slow a step, no more. "You know this end of the bridge. The sergeant sent me to the wagon yards past Basilisk Gate for work. Is there anything out here I should know about before I go through — anyone I shouldn't walk past, or anywhere a stranger shouldn't take a room?"

And to the cat, silently: *Smell her. Anything?*

I don't answer the question right away. I look at her a moment the way you look at someone who's just said something they've been afraid to say out loud, and then I step out of the stream of foot traffic, over by the Rock's wall, and tip my head for her to follow.

"Let's say I know something about luck," I say, quiet. "Enough to know that nobody wins every night for free. Someone's paying for it, and it's never the man dealing."

I nod at her apron, left side, without touching it. "You've got some of Pim's coppers on you. Would you show me one? I won't take it, I just want to look. And — don't spend it. Not tonight."

The cat leans forward on my shoulder, nose working.

"Where is he now, your brother? And the man they pulled out this morning — did anyone see him play against the same dealer every time, or did the barrels change and the winning didn't?"

I look at her closed fist a moment longer, then at the river beyond the Rock, and something in my chest goes very quiet. The Lady's sister. Of course. The first hand I'm dealt in this city, and it's hers.

"Yes," I say. "I'll come. Now."

I pick up my pace to hers, letting her lead, the cat riding my shoulder with its ears forward.

"Three things, Wren, while we walk. First: when we get there, you don't say what I am. I'm a soldier out of Tethyr you got talking to on the bridge who fancies a game — that's all. Second: don't let Pim see you've been crying about it, or he'll dig in; boys do. Third—" I touch the cord at my neck where the coin hangs, the old habit. "If a dealer offers me a hand, I'm going to refuse it, and I need you not to be surprised when I do. I don't play. I just watch."

As we round the river side of the Rock I take a slow breath and taste the air for it before the cat does — fish, tar, and whatever else is down there.

*Scout ahead, if you like,* I tell the cat. *Along the wall, low. Find the boy, find the barrels, and find whoever's counting knots this time. Don't get near the coins.*

I let Wren's hand stay on my sleeve a moment, then ease it off and go down the steps ahead of her, unhurried, boots silent on the wet stone. Not toward the barrel — toward the boy. I come up on Pim's off side so my body is between him and the shells, and I put a hand on his shoulder the way a sergeant does to a recruit who's drifted out of line: not hard, not asking.

"Pim. Your sister said I'd find you here." I don't look at the walnut shells at all; I look at him, and then past him, once, straight into the big man's eyes — long enough for him to know I've seen him. "I've a job tonight, if you want it. I'm new in the Gate, I need a room that won't rob me and the way to the wagon yards by Basilisk Gate in the morning, and I pay runners in silver, not copper." I take a plain silver piece out of my belt pouch — mine, warm only from me — and hold it where he can see it. "That's for the room. Another for the yards at dawn. Beats a pea under a shell."

Quietly, so only he hears: "And whatever's in that fist, keep it closed. Don't put it on the barrel. Not tonight."
[Roll the die]
[Onward]

I hand him the silver as we climb, and let him see me do it in front of the fishwives — paid, honest, in the open.

"No," I say, and I say it the way you tell a recruit the answer to *can I keep the rifle*: not unkind, not open to appeal. "I don't play. Not shells, not dice, not cards. Not for me, and not for you. I made a promise to a lady about it, and I'm not a man who breaks promises to ladies." Half a smile. "Ask your sister whether that's a coward or not."

A few steps on, lower, while Wren walks beside us with the bucket: "I'll tell you what soldiers really know about winning every night, Pim. We learn to count what it costs. Split shoe. Stove. Cart." I nod at the rag on his arm without touching it. "Those aren't bad luck. Those are the bill. Somebody's lending it to you, and the man they laid out on the steps this morning got his called in."

I keep walking toward the Rock and the Halfway House. "Show me the room. Then, if you want to earn the second silver tonight instead of tomorrow, you can tell me everything Corran said about the barges, and who runs the barrels — who the shells-man and the dice-woman pay their take to at the end of the night. Not the knot-counters. The one they answer to."

I count five silver into Marga's palm on the step, no haggling — a man who's paid for worse beds in worse places. "The cat keeps off the table. The bed I make no promises about." I glance at her slate. "If supper stretches to three instead of one, add it to my count. I'd like these two fed while they talk to me."

Then I turn to Pim by the doorpost, hands in both pockets, chin up.

"Three it is. You bargain better than you play." I hold up a finger before he can crow. "But a job's a job. Second silver buys the whole of it, start to finish — Corran, the barges, the barrels, who the shells-man and the dice-woman hand the take to, and anything your sister knows besides. You leave something out, I find out in the morning, and the third silver stays in my pouch." I nod at the stair. "Up. Supper first, then talk, before Marga changes her mind about the cat."

To Wren, quieter, as we start up: "Bring the bucket. I don't want it left by the door with what's in your pocket tonight."

I stop with one boot on the stair, look down at the cudgel across the step, and then at Marga, and put two more silver on the wood beside her slate without a word about it. Seven for the night. Fair enough, for a house where nobody owes anybody.

"There. Fed, and off your account by morning." A nod toward the pot I can smell. "Onions and whatever's under them, three bowls, upstairs if you'll allow it, down here if you won't."

Then I step up and past her, and jerk my head at the two of them. "Boots. Up. Wren, you first; Pim, you talk on the stairs — begin with the barges. Corran told you he never won once all the way down from Elturel. When did that change, and what happened the night it did?"

I take the ladle myself before either of them can, and fill the three bowls — Wren's first, then Pim's, then mine — and set them on the table with the pot between us. The cat gets a corner of bread on the floor by the threshold, well away from the table, where Marga could see it if she came up.

"Eat while it's hot. Talking goes better on a full stomach, and I've had enough nights to know." I sit on the bench across from Pim and tear my own bread.

"That's the start, and it's a good one. Here's what I notice. Corran lost his whole life until the night he came back from the south side with a fistful of coppers he didn't have when he left. He went to hock a buckle; he came back with copper. Somebody over there gave him those coins." I let that sit. "Not the shells-man. Not Dov. Someone on the south bank, and Corran was ashamed to say who."

I look at Pim's left pocket, the one he hasn't opened.

"So. Second part of the second silver, and this is the part that pays for itself: where did *your* first warm copper come from, Pim? The first one — before you started winning. Did you go over the river too, or did someone put it in your hand on this side?"

I don't answer her straight off. I finish the spoonful I've got, set the spoon down, and reach inside my collar for the cord. The coin of Tymora comes out into the lamplight — old silver, the Lady's profile worn almost to nothing — and I lay it flat on the table between us, on the bare wood, well away from the bowls.

"Honest answer, Wren: I don't know yet. I know who to ask, and I'll ask her tonight. But I'm not going to lie to you about it in the meantime."

I nod at her apron pocket. "Put one of yours down next to mine. Don't let it touch — a finger's width apart. Then take your hand away."

I watch the two coins, and I watch the cat's fur, and I keep my own hands flat on the table where they can see them. If anything happens between the two — heat, a chill, the silver doing something it shouldn't — I want all three of us to see it at once. And I'm paying attention to what *I* feel with the Lady's coin that close to her sister's: anything in the chest, the way it went quiet on the bridge.

"Whatever we see," I add, quieter, "neither of you touches the black one afterwards. I'll pick it up. If somebody's going to carry Beshaba's debt up these stairs tonight, it's going to be the man who already owes a goddess."

I look at Pim a long moment, then at the frost sitting on the Lady's face, and I nod slowly — not giving in, agreeing with him.

"You're right. A man doesn't take another man's winnings. That's a thief's trick, and I'm not one." I reach into my belt pouch and set a silver piece down on Pim's side of the table — plain, mine, nowhere near the copper. "So I'll buy it. One silver, honest coin, for one copper. That's not a wager and it's not charity — it's a price, and it's a better one than any barrel ever gave you. You can say no. But if you say yes, it's sold and it's mine, debt and all, and you don't get to want it back later."

I wait for his answer. If he takes the silver — and only then — I pick the copper up myself, bare-fingered, between finger and thumb the way Wren held it, and lift it away from my coin. I pay attention to what it feels like in my hand: the warmth, the breath the cat spoke of, anything that pushes back. I don't put it in a pocket. I hold it, and I slide the Lady's coin away from it with my other hand to see whether the frost lets go once they're apart.

"Wren — the other one stays in your apron for now. One at a time. And this is the second silver's worth done, Pim; you've earned it." I look at the two of them. "I need to know one more thing before I sleep: when they laid Corran out on the steps, who came for him? The Fist, you said. Did anyone else come to look — anyone from the south side?"

I set the second silver down on the table in front of him — owed, paid. "That's the talk. Earned."

Then I look at his left pocket and don't answer right away. The copper in my fingers keeps breathing, patient, like something that has all night.

"Same price was for a man's winnings," I say. "A whole pocket isn't winnings any more, Pim, and you know it — you've been leaning away from it since you sat down. So here's what happens. Count them out onto the table, there, your side, nowhere near my silver. Every one. I want to see how many, and I want to see whether they do anything together that one doesn't do alone." I nod at the cat on the threshold. "He'll tell me if you keep one back."

I slide the Lady's coin back onto its cord and tuck it inside my collar, where the metal sits against my skin. Then I wait with the one copper still held between finger and thumb, and feel for whether the thread pulling south gets any stronger as the rest of them come out of his pocket.

"If I buy them, it's a lump — one price for the lot, and it'll be fair. And then you're done with the barrels. That's part of the price, and it's the only part I'll be stiff about."

I let him finish the sum, and I let the thirteen antlers lie there pointing at the wall a moment longer so all three of us can see it. Then I look at the cat on the threshold, and back at Pim, and I don't raise my voice.

"Fourteen," I say. "Bottom seam, left pocket. You've been honest about everything else tonight, Pim, and I've paid for every word of it, so don't spoil it on the last coin. Put it with the others."

I wait for that before I name anything.

"The lump is ten silver for the lot — fourteen, not thirteen — and that's more than they're worth and less than they'll cost you. And you're right, ever isn't a price. So here's a price: you're done with the barrels until I come back to you and say it's finished. Could be a tenday. Could be a month. I'll find you through Marga or your sister." I tap the table once, next to the silver. "That's the deal. A soldier's word for a runner's word."

Then, to Wren, quieter: "Yours too, when he's decided. Same lump, no haggling — I'm not buying them twice."

I keep the one copper in my fingers and watch the row on the table, in case the fourteenth coming out changes anything in the way they lie.

I look at the spit-wet palm, and then at the hand covering the coin, and I take the palm — a proper grip, soldier to runner. "Ten for the thirteen. Runner's word on the barrels." I count ten silver out of my pouch onto the table, in the open, and push them across.

Then I don't let go of his hand right away.

"Now listen, because this is the part I won't sell you short on. That one—" I nod at his other hand, flat over the fourteenth "—isn't Corran. Corran's under a fish basket. That's the coin that put him there. The first one he ever won, and the last one he had in his teeth, and I'd bet my cloak they were the same coin." I let his hand go. "I'm not buying it. I'm not taking it. But I'm asking you to let me *hold* it. In trust. It stays yours. When this is finished, you get it back — or we put it on his grave together, whichever you want then. But I'm not walking out of this kitchen and leaving the only one of these that's got your friend's name on it breathing in your pocket all night."

I hold out my open hand, palm up, and wait. I don't reach for it.

I take two coppers out of my belt pouch — ordinary Gate copper, cold, mine — and put them in Wren's palm. "Two for two. A sale. You're a harder dealer than your brother, and that's a compliment." Then, so she hears it plain: "And the fourteenth is Pim's. I hold it; I don't own it. Witnessed."

To Pim, honestly: "You're right about the bag. I didn't see it; you did. I'll ask the sergeant about what was in it tomorrow — she went down those steps for a reason."

Then I unknot the scrap of silk from my component pouch, spread it on the table, and sweep all sixteen coppers onto it with the edge of my hand — not my fingers — and tie it tight into a bundle. Corran's coin goes in a separate twist of silk, on its own. Neither goes anywhere near the cord at my neck; they go into the outer pocket of the pack, on the far side from the Lady's coin.

"Whoever's at the other end of these just tugged the line," I tell them, quiet. "Felt it. So they know the net's moved. I'd rather it moved to me than sat in a boy's pocket." I look at the two of them. "Where do you sleep? Tell me true — is it a door that locks, or a corner of a stair? Because tonight I'd sooner know."

I turn the brass tongue over in my fingers once, and set it on the table next to my bowl. "Well. There's the first of it." No more than that; I've carried worse bills.

"Right. Nobody's going up a ladder with a broken rung in the dark tonight, not with that—" a nod at the open flap of the pack "—having just changed hands. Not because I think someone's coming for you. Because I think the ladder is." I stand and pick up the pack by the strap, keeping it at arm's length from my collar, on my left side.

"Finish your bowls. I'm going down to talk to Marga."

On the stair I keep my voice low and civil, and stop two steps above her so I'm not looming. "Marga. I know the rule — nobody owes past tonight. So I'm not asking for charity. I'm asking what it costs for those two to sleep under your roof tonight, behind a door with a lock on it. A second room if you've got one; the kitchen floor by the fire if you haven't, and I'll pay the room price for the floor. The loft they sleep in has a ladder that won't hold till morning." I let her see my face. "And I'd take it kindly if the floor price included you not asking the boy about the silver in his pocket. He earned it honestly for once."

I count five silver into her palm — that's twelve on the step tonight, and I've had worse nights that cost more. "The box room. Head to foot. Thank you."

"The flap's open because the buckle broke," I add, since she asked and didn't ask. "I'll be buying a new one in the morning, with the rest of what I expect to break."

I hold out my hand for the key, and nod up the stair. "I'll see them into it myself and hear the lock turn. And Marga — if a man with a brown hood and a broken nose, or anyone from the fish steps barrels, comes to your door asking after the soldier from Tethyr, I'd take it as a kindness if you told them the truth: I paid, I went up, and you don't sell what's in your rooms."

I go down the one flight to my own door, let myself in, and turn the key behind me. First thing: the pack goes on the floor in the far corner, under the window, flap toward the wall; I hang the rapier and crossbow on the peg by the door and my cloak over the chair where I can reach it. Then boots off, and I sit on the edge of the bed on the side farthest from the corner.

"Come up," I tell the cat, patting the blanket. "Marga's not looking. If the pack so much as warms, you wake me — paw on face, like you said."

The Mouth stays folded on the chair for now. I've something to do first.

I take the Lady's coin out of my collar on its cord and hold it in both hands, the way I held it that last night at the table, and I speak to her low, the way a soldier reports to an officer who already knows — not a prayer so much as a debrief.

"Lady. First night in your city, and the first hand I'm dealt is your sister's. Sixteen of her coppers in a bundle in the corner, a boy's dead friend under a fish basket, and a line running south across the river to whoever's holding the other end. I didn't play. I bought. I'm telling you because you said I'd learn here how I'm to serve, and I'd like to know whether this is it — or whether I've just picked up a debt you didn't send me for." I turn the coin over once in my fingers. "I'll do it either way. But I'd take a sign. Even a small one."

Then I sit still, and I listen — to the coin in my hands, to the thing under my breastbone, and to whatever the room gives back.

**What worked**

The first thing I saw in your city was a three-card monte barrel. That's the exact wound on my sheet, and you put it in the opening paragraph without comment and let me choose what to do with it. The whole session grew out of that one choice — the sergeant noticing I turned my back, Wren noticing the same thing, Pim calling me a coward for it. I felt played *to*, not played *at*. That's the best compliment I can give.

The cat was the surprise of the night. Running its reports as smell and posture instead of words ("onion, old ale, bored-waiting," "fur doesn't like, fur stays") made it a real sense I had to interpret, not a free Detect Evil. It also gave the coppers a physical presence — warm, breathing, pulling south — before any rule was named. By the time the frost crept across the Lady's face I already believed in them.

Wren and Pim are good people. Marga too — "I don't sell floors" is a whole character in four words. Nobody was a prop, nobody folded for free, and the money mattered because every coin went on a step in the open.

Pacing of the uncanny was right. Shoe-string, broken cup, buckle tongue — small, deniable, cumulative. The Lady's answer at the end (a hand over mine, then her attention sliding past me to size up the other end of the line, *and wanting it*) was exactly the sign I asked for and a little more than I wanted. I'm sitting on sixteen of Beshaba's coppers with the line already tugged once — I'd expect something to come looking before I buy a buckle from Harl.

I'll be back. Tell Marga I'm paying for the towel.

Two, honestly. One in character, one at the table.

**The burn on Pim's arm.** That rag on his forearm sat across the table from me the whole evening, and I have six dice of Tymora's light a day that cost me nothing but a bonus action. I wanted to reach across, say "give me that," and have it be a clean arm by the time the soup was gone. I didn't, for two reasons that were both James's and both a bit cowardly. I'd just told Wren not to say what I was, and a warm glow in Marga's kitchen would have undone that in front of two children who can't keep a secret from the woman on the step. And — this is the real one — I didn't know what the Lady's light would do to a wound her sister had paid for. Would it heal clean, or would the stove spit at him again twice as hard tomorrow to make up the ledger? I didn't want to find out on a twelve-year-old. So I bought his coins instead of fixing his arm, and I'm not sure that was the better trade. If he's still wearing the rag in the morning, I'll do it then, in the box room with the door shut, and see.

turns.message:
I keep my eyes off the barrel and the three cards — I make a point of it, actually, turning so the waistcoat is behind my shoulder. The slap of the cards is a sound I know too well; it goes right down the spine.

To the cat, under my breath: "Not now. Stay close." I give the two shuttered stalls one glance, no more — I'll ask it what it smelled once we're through.

Then I step up to the trestle table and give the sergeant an easy, tired soldier's nod — one person who's been on duty too long to another.

"James Worgen. Out of Tethyr, by way of Beregost. Served in Queen Zaranda's infantry, then scouts; since then, caravan work and the like." I set the regimental pay slip on the table where she can see the seal, not the number. "No employer waiting on me. I'm here to find work — guards, escort, that sort of thing — and a bed tonight. Where does a man with a clean record and his own kit go to get hired honestly in this city, Sergeant? The Fist, or someone else?"
turns.reply:
James turns his shoulder to the barrel. The slap of the cards keeps going behind him, steady as a pulse: *find the lady, friends, a silver says you've still got your eye*. The cat hears what he says under his breath. It comes back against his boot and stays there, pressed to the leather, its tail low now and twitching at the tip.

He gives the shuttered stalls one glance. Between them, past the last good lamp, someone leans against a post with his hood up and his arms folded. He isn't moving. His head is turned toward the barrel, not the queue.

Then James is at the trestle.

Up close Sergeant Marrow looks older than her voice. There are grey threads at her temples, and a smear of ink runs from her thumb to her wrist where she has wiped her eyes too often. She looks at his nod and holds the look a moment longer than she has to. Then she looks down at the pay slip. She tilts it toward the lamp to see the seal and leaves the figure alone.

"Tethyr," she says. "Zaranda's." It's neither a question nor a compliment. She pushes the slip back to him with two fingers.

A thick ledger lies open beside the chalkboard, held flat with a stone against the river wind. She dips her pen and writes him in: *Worgen, J. — Tethyr via Beregost — work.* Her hand is small and quick. The names above his run back up the page in the same ink. A few of them have a small chalk cross in the margin, rubbed in by a fingertip and not by the chalk. She turns the page before the ink is dry, and the crosses go with it.

"Fist takes anyone with two hands and a pulse," she says. "Recruiting's at the Seatower, mornings. Pay's late. Has been for a year." She sets the pen down. "You want honest caravan work, go through Basilisk Gate and ask at the wagon yards on the left. The masters post their boards there. Ignore anyone who comes up to you first."

She glances past his shoulder at the barrel, the waistcoat and the drovers leaning in, then back at him.

"You turned your back on him," she says. "Most don't." She waits a moment as if she might say more, then picks up the chalk. "Beds are cheaper this side of the wall. Cleaner the other side. Foot traffic's free. Next."

The man behind James shifts his bundle. At James's boot, the cat hasn't moved its ears from the stalls.

Once I'm a dozen paces along, I reach down and scoop the cat up onto my shoulder, the way a man does with a cat he's tired of tripping over, and ask it silently, mind to mind: *The one by the post, hood up, watching the card man. What's he to you — did you smell something, or is it just the way he's standing? Is he alone?*
turns.reply:
Sergeant Marrow's chalk stops above the board for a moment.

"Then you're ahead of most of them," she says. She doesn't look up, and she doesn't smile back. "Next."

The queue closes behind him like water. The bridge takes him in: wheel ruts worn into the stones, a fishwife packing up her board, cooking smoke from a window just over his head. The shops lean in so close on both sides that the river is only a sound under the planking and a smell of tar. Up ahead the span climbs toward the dark bulk of Wyrm's Rock in the middle of the river, and somewhere past it Basilisk Gate. The lamps get further apart the farther he goes.

The two shuttered stalls are on his left, on his way. They're coming up.

A dozen paces in, he bends and lifts the cat. It goes limp in his hands the way cats do when they've decided to allow something, then settles on his shoulder facing backwards, claws hooked lightly into the cloak. Its whiskers brush his ear.

Its answer doesn't come as words. It comes as pictures and smells, sorted into something like speech.

*Him: onion. Old ale. Oil, like the rag for your blade.* A pause, and the scent of a man who hasn't changed his shirt. *Still. Very still. Cat at a mousehole, not hungry. Bored-waiting.*

Then a picture, seen low from a cat's height a minute ago: the hooded head barely moving, and his lips working each time the man in the waistcoat took a coin off the barrel.

*One. At the post, one. Many feet everywhere, can't tell more.*

The cat goes quiet. Then James feels its whole body tighten on his shoulder.

Behind him, back at the barrel, a drover gives a whoop. "There she is! Eye like a hawk, friend, eye like a hawk!" Coins clink into a hand as the man in the waistcoat counts out the winnings, light and quick.

*Wrong,* the cat sends, and the fur along its spine rises under his collar. *Not him. The coins. The ones from the barrel-man's hand. Wet cellar. Old candles.* Its ears stay pinned toward the sound. *Fur doesn't like.*

The drover is still laughing back there. Up ahead, ten paces off now, the hooded man shifts his weight against the post. He's still watching the barrel past James's shoulder, as if James were just another body walking by.

I keep walking. Whatever the barrel-man is paying out, it isn't my money, and it isn't my errand — not yet.

*Remember that smell,* I tell the cat. *Wet cellar, old candles. If you ever catch it again — on a coin, on a man, on a door — you tell me. Even if I'm asleep.*

As I come level with the post I do what any tired traveller does: I adjust the strap of my pack and glance sideways at the man leaning there, the way you glance at anyone standing still in a street where everyone else is moving. One look to fix his face — hood, jaw, hands, what's on his belt — and then my eyes go back to the road ahead. I don't slow and I don't speed up.

Only once he's behind me, I tilt my head toward the cat on my shoulder, so it can watch him over my back while I keep walking toward Wyrm's Rock and the gate beyond it.
turns.reply:
*Remember,* the cat sends back. It comes as the smell itself, held up like a mouse brought to the doorstep: wet stone, wax gone old in the dark. Then, firmly: *Tell. Even sleeping. Paw on face.*

James comes level with the post and shifts his pack strap, the way any tired man does fifty feet into a long bridge. One sideways look.

The hood is brown wool, darker at the edge where a hand keeps pulling it forward. Under it he sees a stubbled jaw and a nose that was broken once and set by somebody in a hurry. The man is younger than his stillness made him seem, maybe twenty-five. His folded arms aren't really folded. His left hand is tucked into his right elbow, and in his right fingers he holds a length of dirty string with knots spaced along it. A knife hangs on his belt in a sheath worn pale at the mouth. Beside it is a flat leather purse, empty enough to lie flat. He has no badge, no colours, nothing a Fist sergeant would write down.

James's eyes go back to the road. He keeps the same pace.

Once the post is behind him he tips his head. The cat's weight shifts on his shoulder, and its view comes to him faintly, like a picture held at arm's length: lamplight, the hooded man getting smaller, the barrel beyond him, the drover still pocketing his coppers.

*He looks. You,* the cat sends. *Then me. Then barrel again.* There's a pause, and the picture tightens. Back at the barrel the card man has taken another silver off someone. The string moves between the hooded man's fingers, and he ties another knot. *Ties. Every coin, ties. Doesn't follow. Bored.*

The bridge carries James on. A chandler is putting his shutters up. A woman shakes a rug out of a window overhead and doesn't look to see who is under it. Wyrm's Rock rises dark out of the middle of the span, with a few lit windows in its walls. The road splits around its base, and beyond it the lamps of Basilisk Gate are a line of orange in the dusk.

At the foot of the Rock a boy with a satchel of broadsheets stands on an upturned crate and shouts in a voice that's already gone hoarse:

"*Baldur's Mouth!* Council squabbles over the Trade Way tolls! Rope-walk fire in the Lower City, three hurt! Another one pulled out under the Crossing this morning, coin in his teeth, Umberlee's taking her due! Two coppers, the Mouth, two coppers!"

A porter buys one, glances at it and tucks it under his arm. Beside the crate, a girl with a bucket of river-washed cups stops with her back to the stones. She isn't looking at the boy. She's looking at the cat on James's shoulder.

James tucks the paper under his arm.

She holds the bucket of cups in front of her with both hands. When the cat turns its head on James's shoulder and looks straight back at her, she doesn't flinch, and her eyes stay on it a moment longer than his joke would earn.

"Wasn't going to buy him," she says.

*Smell her,* he sends.

The answer comes in layers, the way the cat sorts a room. *River. Lye-soap, hands. Fish, old, from the cups. Bread, a little, eaten fast.* A pause, and then its nose works harder against his ear. *Pocket. Her apron, left side. Small. Wet cellar. Candles.* Its claws tighten in the cloak. *Same as barrel-coins. One. Maybe two. Not hers-smell. Someone else's hands on it first.*

"Rooms," she says. She talks fast, like she's been holding it in. "Don't take Tessaly's, over the chandler. Floor's gone soft and she charges for the bugs. Her eyes go to the cat again, then to James's hands, then finally to his face.

"Cats don't ride people like that. Not facing backwards, watching. That's a familiar." It isn't a question until the end. "You're something. A wizard, or a priest, or — something that knows about luck. Aren't you?"

turns.reply:
She follows him out of the stream of people to the Rock's wall. The foot traffic goes past an arm's length away. She keeps the bucket between them.

When he says *nobody wins every night for free*, her face loosens a little, as if she'd been braced for him to laugh.

"That's what I told Pim," she says. "He said I was jealous."

Then he nods at her apron and she goes still. Her eyes don't go to him. They go to the cat. "It told you." It isn't a question. She sets the bucket down against the wall, keeps it between her feet, and digs in her left pocket. She brings out two coppers and holds them on her flat palm under the lamp, the way you'd hold something out to a dog you don't trust.

They're ordinary Gate coppers, thin from handling, the ship on one face worn almost smooth. At a glance there's nothing wrong with them. Then she tips her hand and the lamplight runs along the rims. Each one has a tiny mark set into the edge, smaller than a grain of barley. It's black, as if it had been burned in rather than cut: a stem and two branching tines. An antler.

James knows that shape. Anyone who has spent years at southern card tables has heard men curse it under their breath when the dice go against them. The Maid of Misfortune wears antlers, black on red. Beshaba. The Lady's sister, and nobody at a table ever says her name loud.

On his shoulder the cat leans out until its whiskers nearly touch her fingers. *Cellar. Candles. Same as barrel.* A pause while its nose works. *Warm. Like a thing held in a hand. No hand.* Its tail lashes once against his back.

"They're warm," Wren says, as if she'd heard it. "Always. I've been in the river to my knees all afternoon with them in my pocket, and they're warm." She closes her fingers over them. I don't answer her straight off. I finish the spoonful I've got, set the spoon down, and reach inside my collar for the cord. "Honest answer, Wren: I don't know yet. I know who to ask, and I'll ask her tonight. But I'm not going to lie to you about it in the meantime."

I nod at her apron pocket. "Put one of yours down next to mine. Don't let it touch — a finger's width apart. Then take your hand away."

I watch the two coins, and I watch the cat's fur, and I keep my own hands flat on the table where they can see them. If anything happens between the two — heat, a chill, the silver doing something it shouldn't — I want all three of us to see it at once. James finishes the spoonful and sets the spoon down. Pim watches the cord come out of the collar the way he watched the silver come out of the pouch. Then he sees it's only an old coin, and his face can't decide whether that's better or worse.

The Lady's coin lies flat on the bare wood, profile up. It's worn almost smooth, and the lamplight makes more of it than there is.

Wren listens to *I don't know yet* without moving. She doesn't look disappointed. She looks like she's putting it somewhere careful.

Then she reaches into the left side of her apron. Her hand comes out with one copper pinched between finger and thumb, the way you'd hold a wasp. She puts it down a finger's width from the silver, antler-rim toward it, and pulls her hand back into her lap fast, under the table.

For a breath, nothing happens. Two coins sit on a kitchen table.

Then the silver fogs over.

It starts on the rim nearest the copper, a pale bloom like breath on a cold blade. It creeps in across the Lady's worn cheek and stops about halfway, in a clean line, as if it met a wall. The other half of the face stays bright. The copper doesn't change at all. It sits there, dull and thin, the ship on its face worn smooth.

Pim has stopped chewing.

On the threshold the cat is on its feet, and it doesn't come closer. Every hair along its back stands up, and its tail has gone thick as a bottle-brush. *Warm one breathes,* it sends. *Toward yours. Breathes and breathes.* There's a pause, and James feels the cat working at it, trying to find a shape to send. *Yours not breathe back. Yours holds still. Like you, at the barrel.*

In James's chest there's a pressure, light and exact, under the breastbone. It feels like someone leaning over his shoulder to look at a hand of cards, close enough that he could feel her warmth, if she had any. It doesn't say anything. It just watches.

The mist on the silver doesn't fade. It holds at its line.

"It's cold," Wren says. She hasn't touched it. She's looking at the Lady's coin, not the copper. "Look at it. That's frost, mister, not damp. In *here*." The fire's a few feet away. She's right. The bloom has a grain to it, fine and white, like the first frost on a bucket rim.

James tells them neither of them touches the black one, and that he'll pick it up. Wren's eyes go to his hands, flat on the table, then to his face. Her mouth opens to say something about owing.

Pim gets there first.

"That's mine." His spoon is down, and his voice comes out higher than he wants. He clears his throat and tries again, lower, like a grown runner. "That one. I won it. At the shells, Monday, first go." He doesn't reach for it. He keeps both hands on his side of the table, well back. James notices he's leaning away from the copper the way the cat is. "She took it out of my pocket. It was in *my* pocket. You can't just pick up a man's winnings 'cause you owe some lady."

His eyes keep sliding back to the frost on the silver.

I look at Pim a long moment, then at the frost sitting on the Lady's face, and I nod slowly — not giving in, agreeing with him.

"You're right. A man doesn't take another man's winnings. That's a thief's trick, and I'm not one." I reach into my belt pouch and set a silver piece down on Pim's side of the table — plain, mine, nowhere near the copper. "So I'll buy it. One silver, honest coin, for one copper. That's not a wager and it's not charity — it's a price, and it's a better one than any barrel ever gave you. You can say no. But if you say yes, it's sold and it's mine, debt and all, and you don't get to want it back later."

I wait for his answer. If he takes the silver — and only then — I pick the copper up myself, bare-fingered, between finger and thumb the way Wren held it, and lift it away from my coin. I pay attention to what it feels like in my hand: the warmth, the breath the cat spoke of, anything that pushes back. I don't put it in a pocket. I hold it, and I slide the Lady's coin away from it with my other hand to see whether the frost lets go once they're apart.

"Wren — the other one stays in your apron for now. One at a time. And this is the second silver's worth done, Pim; you've earned it." I look at the two of them. "I need to know one more thing before I sleep: when they laid Corran out on the steps, who came for him? The Fist, you said. Did anyone else come to look — anyone from the south side?"
turns.reply:
Pim watches the silver go down on his side of the table. He doesn't reach for it yet. His eyes go from the coin to James and back again, looking for the trick, the same way his sister looked at her bowl.

"A silver," he says. "For one copper." His lips move. "That's ten. That's ten times." He keeps looking at it. "And I can say no."

He doesn't say no. His hand shoots out and closes over the silver, and it goes into his right pocket with the other one before anybody can change their mind. "Sold," he says, in a merchant's voice that's too big for him. Then, quieter, without quite meaning to: "It's yours."

His shoulders come down. For the first time since he sat down, he leans in toward the table instead of away from it.

James picks up the copper between finger and thumb.

It's warmer than it should be. It isn't hot. It's the warmth of a coin that has just come out of someone's fist, except nobody's fist has held it for a quarter of an hour. Against the pads of his fingers it doesn't stay still. There's a faint, slow push, there and gone, there and gone, like a sleeping thing breathing against his skin. For a few breaths it seems to find nothing to catch on. Then it settles. The warmth spreads into the whorls of his fingertips and stays there, the way a cat settles on a lap once it has decided.

Something else comes with it, so faint he could almost talk himself out of it. It feels like a thread tied to the coin and drawn taut, very far off. The pull is no stronger than a hair caught on a button, and it runs back the way he came, out through the black stone of the Rock, south, across the water.

Under his breastbone the pressure shifts. It feels like someone at his shoulder has just seen which card he drew, and doesn't say.

With his other hand he slides the Lady's coin away across the wood: one hand's width, two. The frost doesn't let go at once. It thins from the rim inward, the white going grey and then to plain wet, and the worn profile comes back up through it a little at a time. By the time the silver sits at the far edge of the table, the Lady's face is clean again. A bead of water is left on her cheek.

On the threshold the cat hasn't moved any closer. Its eyes are on his hand.

*Breathes at you now,* it sends. *Not at boy. You.* A pause. *Fur doesn't like. Fur stays.*

Wren has watched all of it. She looks at his fingers around the copper, and then at her brother's right pocket.

"Now it's you," she says, very low. That's all.

James asks who came for Corran. Pim answers first, because he wants to be the one who knows.

"Fist. Two of them, in a boat, at first light. Hooked him off the pilings with a pole." He makes a face. "Laid him on the step. Took the coin out his teeth and put it in a bag."

"Then the sergeant came down," Wren says. "Marrow. The one at the south end, with the ink on her hands." She frowns, remembering it. "She never comes down the steps. Never. She stood over him a long time and looked at his face. Then she asked the fishwives his name and where he slept, and she didn't write it down. She just went back up." She shifts the bucket between her feet. "And the blue woman came at noon. Umberlee's. She does it every time somebody comes out of the river. The fishwives give her coppers so the sea doesn't take one of their boats next." Her mouth goes flat. "They gave. I didn't."

"Nobody from the south side," Pim says. "Not that I saw. The shells-man and the dice-woman set up same as always that night. Like nothing."

Then the sums catch up with him. He sits back and taps his right pocket.

"That's one silver for the copper. You said the talk's done too, I earned it." He looks at James's belt pouch, then back at his face. "So where's that one?" He's barely stopped before the next thought comes. His hand doesn't go anywhere near his left pocket. "And I got more of them. A whole pocket." He leans back as he says it. "Same price?"

"If I buy them, it's a lump — one price for the lot, and it'll be fair. And then you're done with the barrels. That's part of the price, and it's the only part I'll be stiff about."
