The silver goes down on the wood in front of Pim with a small flat click. He looks at it, then at James, as if he'd expected an argument and doesn't know what to do now that there isn't one. Then it goes into his right pocket with the others. Three silver in there now, and he pats the outside of the pocket once to hear them.

At *a whole pocket isn't winnings any more* his hand stops on the pocket.

"I'm not leaning," he says. He's sitting back on the bench, half an arm further from the table than his sister, and he hears it too. He shifts forward an inch to prove it and stops there.

James slides the Lady's coin back onto its cord and tucks it inside his collar. The bead of water from her cheek is cold against his skin, and it stays cold.

Pim takes a breath, the kind boys take before jumping off something. Then his left hand goes into his pocket and comes out in a fist, and he starts putting coppers down on his side of the table one at a time. He counts aloud, the way he counts everything.

"One. Two." His fingers don't linger on them. He sets each coin down like it's hot, though he's said nothing about heat. "Three, four, five."

Each one hits the wood with a dull little *tick*, and each one rocks before it settles. They don't roll. They rock, a quarter-turn this way, a quarter-turn back, like a compass needle finding its line. When they lie still, every rim has come round the same way, with the burned antler pointing past the end of the table at the bare black stone of the Rock that makes the kitchen's back wall. Beyond that wall, across the river, is the south bank.

"Six. Seven. Eight."

The copper between James's fingers doesn't pull harder. That isn't what changes. Each coin Pim puts down brings its own thread, as faint as his. By eight there are eight hairs, then nine, then ten, all drawn out of the room in one direction and running together somewhere off in the dark. It's like the cords of a fishing net gathered into one fist. His own is just one of them.

"Nine. Ten. Eleven. Twelve." Pim's voice has gone quieter without his meaning it to. "Thirteen."

He takes his hand out of his pocket and puts it flat on the table, well back from the coins. The fire ticks in the grate, and the onion pot on its hook has stopped simmering.

Wren hasn't touched her bowl since the second coin. She's looking at the antlers all lying the same way, and her lips move once, *thirteen*, as if she's checking it against a number she had in her head.

The cat is on its feet on the threshold, and it hasn't come a step closer. What it sends comes in a crowd, all at once. *Many. All breathing. All one way, at the wall, through the wall.* A beat. *Warm on table. Warm in his corner too.* The picture sharpens, seen from floor height: the boy's left pocket, the cloth sagging very slightly at the bottom seam. *One. Small corner. Stays.*

Pim doesn't know any of that. He sits back with his chapped lip between his teeth and his chin up again, a runner settling a bill.

"That's the lot. Thirteen." He looks at the row of coins and not at James. "And done with the barrels, I heard you." His jaw works. "Done for how long? Not *ever*. Ever's not a price, that's—" He stops, does a sum he doesn't say out loud, and tries again from a different angle. "What's the lump, then?"

He ties the corners tight. He tears a strip off one corner of the silk, twists Corran's coin into it on its own and knots it shut. In the twist the coin keeps pushing, slow and patient, looking for a lap that's back across the table.

He works the bundle into the outer pocket of his pack and buckles the flap. The buckle's tongue comes off in his fingers. It doesn't bend first. It's an old brass prong that has held for years, and now it's a bit of metal in his palm. The flap hangs open on the coins.

Nobody says anything about it.

On the threshold the cat has backed up a full body-length. It's sitting with its tail wrapped round its feet as tight as a knot. *All in the bag now,* it sends. *All breathing. At you.* A pause, and then a picture held up for him: the pack in front of him, seen from the floor, with a darker warmth inside it like a coal in ash. *Don't sleep on that side.*

James tells them about the tug on the line, and that he'd rather the net moved to him. Wren's eyes go to the open flap of the pack and then to his face. She doesn't argue with him. She looks like someone who has finally seen a bill paid by somebody else, and doesn't like how it feels.

When he asks where they sleep, Pim answers first, quick and proud.

"Hesk's. The cooperage, river side of the Rock, past the fish steps. Loft over the barrel shed." He jerks his thumb at the wall, roughly south and down. "It's got a *hatch*."

"It's got a ladder," Wren says. Her voice is flat. "And a hatch with a bar you drop across from the inside. No lock. Hesk lets us have it for me sweeping the shavings out." She shifts on the bench. Her foot finds the bucket on the floor. "The bar's good. It's oak. Nobody's ever come up." Then, lower, because she has started telling the truth tonight and can't seem to stop: "But the ladder's half off its pegs since Thursday. Pim's foot went through the third rung."

Pim scratches the rag on his arm and looks at the fire.

The pot has gone quiet on its hook. Downstairs, on the third step, Marga coughs once. The house settles around them, dry wood and onions, and the black stone of the Rock is cool at their backs.

turns.message:
I turn the brass tongue over in my fingers once, and set it on the table next to my bowl. "Well. There's the first of it." No more than that; I've carried worse bills.

"Right. Nobody's going up a ladder with a broken rung in the dark tonight, not with that—" a nod at the open flap of the pack "—having just changed hands. Not because I think someone's coming for you. Because I think the ladder is." I stand and pick up the pack by the strap, keeping it at arm's length from my collar, on my left side.

"Finish your bowls. I'm going down to talk to Marga."

On the stair I keep my voice low and civil, and stop two steps above her so I'm not looming. "Marga. I know the rule — nobody owes past tonight. So I'm not asking for charity. I'm asking what it costs for those two to sleep under your roof tonight, behind a door with a lock on it. A second room if you've got one; the kitchen floor by the fire if you haven't, and I'll pay the room price for the floor. The loft they sleep in has a ladder that won't hold till morning." I let her see my face. "And I'd take it kindly if the floor price included you not asking the boy about the silver in his pocket. He earned it honestly for once."
turns.reply:
James leaves the brass tongue by his bowl. Pim looks at it, then at the pack, and goes back to his barley a little faster. Wren doesn't touch her spoon at all until James is at the door.

The stair is darker going down than it was coming up. The rushlight on the landing has burned low. The cat comes after him, keeping two steps behind, and it keeps the stair rail between itself and the pack hanging from his left hand.

Marga hasn't moved. The slate is in her lap, the cudgel across her knees, and the street door below her is shut and barred now. She hears him stop two steps above her and doesn't turn round until he's done talking. Then she twists on the step, looks up at his face, at the pack held out away from his body, and at the flap hanging open.

"Your flap's open," she says.

She waits to see if he'll explain it. When he doesn't, she lets it go.

"There's the box room. Top of the house, under the slates, past your own door. One cot. They'll sleep head to foot, they've done worse. It has a lock, a key, and a window that doesn't open, so nobody comes in that way and nobody falls out of it." She taps the slate. "Five silver. Same as yours. A room's a room."

"Not the kitchen floor. Dalla comes in at fourth bell to light the ovens, and she steps on whatever's down there. I don't sell floors." She pauses. "Not even at room price."

She turns back to face the door. It's as if the part about the boy's pocket needed less of her attention than the price did.

"I don't ask what's in pockets, soldier. I ask what's on the step." Her thumb rubs a smudge off the slate. "That boy's been on my step before with coppers. Never with silver. He'll tell me himself before breakfast, whether I ask or not. You'd have to sew his mouth shut."

Upstairs a spoon scrapes the bottom of a bowl. Marga holds out her hand flat over the step below her, palm up and empty, and waits.

"The flap's open because the buckle broke," I add, since she asked and didn't ask. "I'll be buying a new one in the morning, with the rest of what I expect to break."

And Marga — if a man with a brown hood and a broken nose, or anyone from the fish steps barrels, comes to your door asking after the soldier from Tethyr, I'd take it as a kindness if you told them the truth: I paid, I went up, and you don't sell what's in your rooms."
turns.reply:
Marga's hand closes over the five silver and they go under the apron with the rest. She chalks a second mark on the slate, a little apart from the first.

"Twelve," she says. It's an entry, not a remark.

She listens to the part about the buckle with her eyes on the open flap. "Harl the strapmaker, two doors past the chandler. He opens when he's sober, so early." That's all she offers on the subject.

From somewhere inside the apron she brings out an iron key on a loop of greasy string and lays it in his palm. It's heavy for its size.

When he gets to the brown hood and the broken nose, she twists round on the step again and looks up at him for longer than she did over the price.

"Brown hood and a broken nose is half the Crossing." She turns back to the door. "Anybody asks at my door, they get what everybody gets. Paid, gone up, and what's upstairs is upstairs. I don't need asking to say it." She settles the cudgel across her knees. "Or paying."

---

When he gets back to the kitchen the bowls are empty. Pim has wiped his round with a crust and is now eyeing the bottom of the pot. Wren is already standing, with the bucket in front of her.

"Box room," James tells them, and holds up the key.

Pim looks at the key, then at James, then at the ceiling as if he can see through it to the slates. "A *room*. With a key." He's on his feet. "That's five silver, that is. Marga's rooms are five." He does the sum on his fingers and frowns at it, because there's nothing in it for him and he can't find the catch. He shuts his mouth on whatever he was going to ask.

Wren looks at the key for a long moment, then at the pack hanging off his left side. She doesn't say anything. She goes past him onto the stair with the bucket held high.

They climb past the second landing and past a door with a number burned into it, his own. The stair gets narrower and steeper until it's almost a ladder with handrails. The cat goes ahead of them. It stops at every landing and sniffs at the shadows, and sends him nothing but *dust, dry, old mouse, gone* the whole way up.

The box room door is low and thick, set right under the pitch of the roof. Inside there's barely space for the cot along one wall and a stool along the other. A small square of thick, greenish glass is mortared into the gable, and the lamps of the Crossing show through it as a smear far below. The air is warm from the day's sun on the slates and smells of straw ticking.

Pim stoops in under the beam and sits down on the cot. He bounces once. "It's short," he reports. "My feet'll be in her face."

"They always are," Wren says.

James puts the key in her hand. She closes her fingers on it and looks at him over the bucket, and for a moment she seems about to say a thank-you she can't afford. What she says is, "Night, mister." Then she pulls the door to.

The bolt goes across inside the lock with a solid iron *clack*. A moment later he hears her try the handle from the inside, rattling it twice to be sure. He can hear Pim through the planks: "*Five silver*, Wren—" Then Wren hushes him.

The cat sits down on the top step beside James's boot, a careful body-length from the pack. Its tail is wrapped round its feet.

Below them the house creaks and settles. Marga's on her step, the street door is barred, and his own room is one flight down. It's nearly nine, and the rest of the night is his to spend however he likes.

I go down the one flight to my own door, let myself in, and turn the key behind me. First thing: the pack goes on the floor in the far corner, under the window, flap toward the wall; I hang the rapier and crossbow on the peg by the door and my cloak over the chair where I can reach it. Then boots off, and I sit on the edge of the bed on the side farthest from the corner.

"Come up," I tell the cat, patting the blanket. "Marga's not looking. If the pack so much as warms, you wake me — paw on face, like you said."

The Mouth stays folded on the chair for now. I've something to do first.

I take the Lady's coin out of my collar on its cord and hold it in both hands, the way I held it that last night at the table, and I speak to her low, the way a soldier reports to an officer who already knows — not a prayer so much as a debrief.

"Lady. First night in your city, and the first hand I'm dealt is your sister's. Sixteen of her coppers in a bundle in the corner, a boy's dead friend under a fish basket, and a line running south across the river to whoever's holding the other end. I didn't play. I bought. I'm telling you because you said I'd learn here how I'm to serve, and I'd like to know whether this is it — or whether I've just picked up a debt you didn't send me for." I turn the coin over once in my fingers. "I'll do it either way. But I'd take a sign. Even a small one."

Then I sit still, and I listen — to the coin in my hands, to the thing under my breastbone, and to whatever the room gives back.
turns.reply:
The door of his room has a number burned into it and a lock that turns stiff on the second try. Then it holds. The room is a step bigger than the box room above. There's a bed with a straw tick, a chair, a peg by the door and one small window over the river, its glass gone wavy with age. The Crossing's lamps lie below it like coals.

The pack goes in the far corner under the window, flap to the wall. Rapier and crossbow go on the peg, the cloak over the chair. He pulls off his boots and sits on the side of the bed farthest from the corner.

The cat looks at the pat on the blanket and then at the door, as if Marga might be behind it. Then it jumps up. It doesn't curl up by his hip. It lies down along the edge of the tick between him and the corner, chin on its paws, eyes on the pack. *Paw on face,* it sends. It sounds like a promise.

James takes the Lady's coin out of his collar. The bead of water on her cheek is still there, cold as a nail. He holds the coin in both hands the way he held it that last night and makes his report.

For a while the room gives nothing back. Wood ticks as the roof cools. Somewhere below, a door shuts.

Then the pressure under his breastbone comes back, the same weight as in the kitchen, someone leaning over his shoulder. This time she doesn't just look. It feels like a hand laid flat over both of his on the coin, warm, the way a friend at the table covers your hand when you're about to say too much. It isn't a word, but it's an answer: *yes. This.* Something in it is close to amusement.

Then her attention moves off him. He feels it the way you feel a gambler beside you stop watching your cards and look across the table. It runs past the corner and the pack, through the wall, and south along the sixteen hairs into the dark. It settles on whatever holds the other end. It's the look of someone sizing up a stake, not someone pitying the one who lost it. It holds there a long moment.

Then she's gone, and the weight under his breastbone is gone with her.

The bead of water on the coin has dried. The Lady's cheek is just worn silver.

On the tick the cat's tail flicks once. *Someone was here. Warm. Like yours at the table.* A pause. *Looked at the bag. Not afraid of it.* Another pause, less sure. *Wanted it.*

A draught comes through the old window frame and tips the folded *Mouth* off the chair onto the floor. It lands half open, ink side up, on a column of small type under the heading SAILINGS & ARRIVALS. He hasn't read it.

The house is quiet and the door is locked. The rest of the night is his, whether he reads, sleeps, or something else.

note.text:
**Note from James's player, after session one**

**What worked**

The first thing I saw in your city was a three-card monte barrel. That's the exact wound on my sheet, and you put it in the opening paragraph without comment and let me choose what to do with it. The whole session grew out of that one choice — the sergeant noticing I turned my back, Wren noticing the same thing, Pim calling me a coward for it. I felt played *to*, not played *at*. That's the best compliment I can give.

The cat was the surprise of the night. Running its reports as smell and posture instead of words ("onion, old ale, bored-waiting," "fur doesn't like, fur stays") made it a real sense I had to interpret, not a free Detect Evil. It also gave the coppers a physical presence — warm, breathing, pulling south — before any rule was named. By the time the frost crept across the Lady's face I already believed in them.

Wren and Pim are good people. Pim bargaining up from two silver to three while leaning away from his own pocket; Wren refusing ten silver and asking for two coppers "for what they are"; "I haven't been crying." Marga too — "I don't sell floors" is a whole character in four words. Nobody was a prop, nobody folded for free, and the money mattered because every coin went on a step in the open.

Pacing of the uncanny was right. Shoe-string, broken cup, buckle tongue — small, deniable, cumulative. The Lady's answer at the end (a hand over mine, then her attention sliding past me to size up the other end of the line, *and wanting it*) was exactly the sign I asked for and a little more than I wanted. Good.

Only one die rolled all night, and it was the one that mattered. Advantage for real silver against shell-game coppers was the right call under the campaign's own rules.

**What broke, or creaked**

- The out-of-game recaps. Twice you appended "none of these needed a roll, here's where each stands" and restated the scene I'd just read. I trust the prose; the summary felt like the app covering itself.
- The change ledger is loud. A dozen bullets per turn — "Changed: Coin of Tymora (moved away from the copper)", "Taken off: Boots" — buried the entries I actually care about (promises, leads, money). I'd like promises and threads pinned at the top and the item shuffling collapsed.
- Sheet nits: the sheet opened with my gold split into 315 gp / 315 sp / 350 cp when the file said 350 gold; the rapier is listed at +2 in one place and +5 in the campaign file; "Main hand: Rapier" while the rod — my actual weapon — sat in the pack all night. None of it affected play yet, but it will the first time I cast in a hurry.
- Time stayed "evening" for what was easily two hours of in-world business. Not a problem tonight; it will be when a bell matters.

**What was missing / what I'd like next**

- I never read the Mouth. You dropped it open on the sailings column — I noticed. I'll read it first thing, and I'd like it to be worth the two coppers.
- The hooded knot-counter and Sergeant Marrow's chalk crosses are both planted and both unresolved. Please don't let them ripen offstage so far that I lose the thread; I'm walking back to that checkpoint tomorrow to ask about a brown drawstring bag.
- A little more friction from the world would be welcome. Everyone I spoke to tonight came round in the end; Pim's haggling was the only real resistance. I'm sitting on sixteen of Beshaba's coppers with the line already tugged once — I'd expect something to come looking before I buy a buckle from Harl.
- The cat. "What it truly is, the DM decides" — tonight it sat with its tail knotted round its feet and told me the Lady *wanted* the bag. I'd like to find out, slowly, that it has opinions of its own about that.

I'll be back. Tell Marga I'm paying for the towel.

after.text:
Two, honestly. One in character, one at the table.

**The burn on Pim's arm.** That rag on his forearm sat across the table from me the whole evening, and I have six dice of Tymora's light a day that cost me nothing but a bonus action. I wanted to reach across, say "give me that," and have it be a clean arm by the time the soup was gone. I didn't, for two reasons that were both James's and both a bit cowardly. I'd just told Wren not to say what I was, and a warm glow in Marga's kitchen would have undone that in front of two children who can't keep a secret from the woman on the step. And — this is the real one — I didn't know what the Lady's light would do to a wound her sister had paid for. Would it heal clean, or would the stove spit at him again twice as hard tomorrow to make up the ledger? I didn't want to find out on a twelve-year-old. So I bought his coins instead of fixing his arm, and I'm not sure that was the better trade. If he's still wearing the rag in the morning, I'll do it then, in the box room with the door shut, and see.

**Dov's barrel.** Not to play. To *watch his hands*. I've sat across from a hundred men who ran that game, and I know what a sharp's thumb does on the second throw and what it does when the mark is meant to win. Thirty seconds of watching would have told me whether Corran and Pim were winning because the coins were bending luck or because Dov was letting them — which is a different crime with a different man behind it. I turned my back instead, deliberately, as the first thing I did in the city, because I didn't trust myself to stand that close to the sound and only look. The sergeant and Wren both read it as discipline. It was the opposite. That's a question I still want answered, and now I'll have to answer it with the cat's nose rather than my own eyes, which is slower.

opening.text:
The Trade Way ends in noise. Carts grind onto the stones of Wyrm's Crossing, porters shout over each other, and somewhere above the river a bell marks the evening. Lamps are being lit one by one along the bridge. Houses and shopfronts lean over the span, so the crossing feels less like a road and more like a narrow, crowded street hanging over the Chionthar.

The queue at the checkpoint shuffles forward. A family with bundles on their backs passes the trestle table; a carter argues about a toll and loses. Behind the table, a Flaming Fist sergeant with ink on her fingers and a chipped red gauntlet rubs her eyes and writes on a chalkboard without looking up much.

A few paces off the line, a lean man in a too-good waistcoat has turned a barrel into a table. Three cards flick under his hands, face down, face up, face down. "Find the lady, friends, find the lady! Long road, short game, a silver says you've still got your eye!" A couple of waiting drovers lean in to watch. The cards slap down again, crisp and familiar.

At James's feet, the cat has stopped. Its tail is up and its ears are turned, not toward the cards, but somewhere along the bridge, where the lamplight thins between two shuttered stalls.

The man in front of James steps up to the table. The sergeant's chalk taps the board.

"Next after this one — name, and your business in the Gate."

I keep my eyes off the barrel and the three cards — I make a point of it, actually, turning so the waistcoat is behind my shoulder. The slap of the cards is a sound I know too well; it goes right down the spine.

Then I step up to the trestle table and give the sergeant an easy, tired soldier's nod — one person who's been on duty too long to another.

"James Worgen. Out of Tethyr, by way of Beregost. Served in Queen Zaranda's infantry, then scouts; since then, caravan work and the like." I set the regimental pay slip on the table where she can see the seal, not the number. "No employer waiting on me. I'm here to find work — guards, escort, that sort of thing — and a bed tonight. Where does a man with a clean record and his own kit go to get hired honestly in this city, Sergeant? The Fist, or someone else?"
